## Keep or rush

In class order. Planned total 75 of the 80 minutes. The class is open
first, then constructive: students say what interests or worries them
about AI, then work as ethics committees writing guidelines.

| Item | Min | | If short |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Discussion 1, open floor: what about AI are you most interested in, or most worried about | 25 | Keep | Fifteen minutes; go to the themes as soon as the board has four |
| The turn: what would have to be true for the worry to be smaller | 5 | Keep | One theme only |
| Discussion 2, an ethics committee: at most five guidelines for one setting | 30 | Keep | Three guidelines, answering questions 2, 3 and 5 |
| Swap and stress test | 10 | Rush | One group reads its guidelines; the room attacks them |
| Close: one guideline, and who it must be justified to | 5 | Keep | One sentence per group |

: {tbl-colwidths="[44,6,10,40]"}

Minimum class: the open floor to its themes, then each committee
writes three guidelines and one is stress-tested by the room.

Fallback. Switch to the items under "If there is time" if the room is
quiet after two prompts, if two or three voices dominate, or if the
open floor is still only complaint after 25 minutes. In order of
preference: discussion 3 (who answers for it, 14 minutes), problem 1
(the endoscopists, 16 minutes with feedback), discussion 4 (you sign
the report, 10 minutes). They also fill a class in which the committees
finish early.

## If you read on

- Open the
  [complete class sheet](https://ethics4ds.com/teachers/wk09/class_complete.html)
  on screen: green boxes are hints, blue boxes are answers and
  directions. The exercises at the top are for students' own time.
- The open floor. Say the ground rule aloud: nobody is asked how they
  use AI themselves. Write what students say on the board in their
  words and group it into themes. Do not correct or answer yet; the
  aim is that the room hears what its members think. If someone
  raises something personal or distressing (the lecture included a
  death), acknowledge it, do not probe, and move to the theme it
  belongs to. If the room is slow, ask pairs to report their
  partner's answer.
- The turn is the hinge of the class. For a theme on the board, ask
  what would have to be true for the worry to be smaller, and who
  could make it true. The answers are conditions, which is what the
  committees then write.
- The committees. Each group takes a different setting; with more
  than five groups, two can share one and report separately. Push for
  guidelines that someone could check: "used responsibly" cannot be
  checked, "every decision letter names the person who reviewed it"
  can. The six questions each lead to an idea from the course
  (validity and tasks in use; levels of abstraction and who signs;
  disclosure; who bears the errors; Goodhart's law; who can say no);
  the directions box has a line on each. Students should reach for
  these themselves before the box is opened.
- The stress test. Groups read another committee's guidelines as
  someone the guidelines would hurt or someone who wants to get
  around them. Question 5 has usually prepared them for this.
- Problem 1 uses two studies from the reading's supplement. The
  Polish study is a before-and-after comparison; the Norwegian one
  withdrew AI by design. Neither settles the question, and the
  solution says so.
- Discussion 3's medical-advice case is an allegation in a lawsuit
  that has not been decided. Say so if a group takes it.
- Every item ends with a question about who bears the cost, who
  gains, or who the choice could be justified to. A group that has
  its guidelines and skips that question has not finished.
- The sheet has no task for next time: the next week's task comes
  with its readings.
